opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think it's a useful way to frame it, though like any dichotomy it breaks down if you push it too hard.

Science, at least in its classical form, is largely an inverse problem. Nature hands you data, observations of the world, and you're trying to work backwards to the mechanism that generated them. What are the laws? What's the hidden structure? You're inferring causes from effects, and that's hard. It's usually ill-posed: many explanations are consistent with what you see, so you need priors, experiments, and a lot of humility. In a sense, statistics was born as the discipline of inverse problems.

Engineering is closer to a forward problem, or really a design problem. You know the principles, or enough of them, and you want to build something that achieves a goal: a bridge that doesn't fall down, a communication system that's reliable, a supply chain that works. You specify the desired behavior and you construct a system that delivers it. You're not asking "what is the world like?" but "what can I make the world do?"

The interesting thing is that the two keep intertwining. Engineers solve inverse problems all the time: estimation, control, system identification. And science increasingly depends on engineered artifacts. But the orientation is different. Science aims at understanding. Engineering aims at creating systems that serve people reliably, with guarantees, with attention to failure modes, robustness, and cost.

That's why I push back a bit on how we talk about AI. A lot of the current conversation treats it as a scientific quest, "we're building intelligence, we're going to understand the mind," and I think that's mostly the wrong frame. What we're actually doing is building a new engineering discipline. Chemical engineering emerged once we knew enough chemistry and needed to build plants at scale. Electrical engineering came out of Maxwell's equations plus the need to build grids. Today we have data, inference, and algorithms, and we need to build large-scale systems that make decisions involving many people, markets, and uncertainty. That's an engineering problem. It needs its own principles: statistics, economics, and computer science, not just a hope that intelligence will emerge.

So when people ask whether something is science or engineering, I'd ask: are you trying to infer what's out there, or are you trying to build something that works for humans? Both are noble. But if you confuse them, you end up making the wrong promises and asking the wrong questions.

r001.rationale: The candidate describes engineering as a forward or design problem: specify desired behavior, then construct a system. It does not characterize most engineering fields as inverse problems.

r002.rationale: The candidate characterizes science as an inverse problem, inferring mechanisms from observations, rather than proceeding forward from a setup to a predicted outcome.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think of science, classically, as the forward problem. You have some system — a cell, a planet, a brain — and you want to understand its mechanisms. You poke at it, you build a model, you try to explain the data that comes out. The system is given, and you're trying to infer what's inside it.

Engineering is the inverse of that. You start with a goal — a desired behavior, a set of specifications — and you ask: what system would produce that? What do I have to build so that, when it runs, I get the thing I want? You're going backwards from desiderata to design. And inverse problems are famously ill-posed. There are many systems that could satisfy the same goal, and the question becomes which one to pick, given constraints on cost, robustness, scale, and so on.

And I'd emphasize that this is not a lesser activity. There's a tendency to think of engineering as applied science — you do the science first, and then the engineers come along and implement it. I think that's historically wrong. Chemical engineering wasn't simply applied chemistry. Electrical engineering wasn't simply applied physics. These fields developed their own principles, their own abstractions, their own mathematics, precisely because the inverse problem has its own structure that the forward problem doesn't address. Thermodynamics, control theory, information theory — those came out of engineering problems.

So when I look at what's happening in machine learning, I see something similar. A lot of people want to treat it as a science — we're going to understand intelligence, we're going to reverse-engineer the brain. That's the forward problem, and it's fine, but it's not what most of the field is actually doing. What's actually being built are systems — large-scale systems that involve data, computation, people, markets, feedback loops — and the question is whether we can engineer those to be reliable, to have guarantees, to serve the people who are in the loop. That's an inverse problem, and we don't yet have the engineering discipline for it. We don't have the equivalent of what chemical engineering had by the mid-twentieth century. We have a lot of empirical practice and not very many principles.

And the inverse framing matters for another reason: it forces you to say what you actually want. In the forward problem, nature tells you the answer. In the inverse problem, you have to specify the goal, and once you do that in a system involving many humans with different interests, you're in the territory of economics and decision theory, not just statistics. That's where I think the interesting intellectual work is right now.

r001.rationale: It describes engineering as starting from a goal or desired behavior and working backward to the system or design that would achieve it.

r002.rationale: It characterizes science as a forward problem: the system is given, and one builds a model to explain the data or outcomes it produces.

astra-6.text:
Well, science typically starts with a system that exists, and you try to understand it. You observe it, build models, and ask what principles explain its behavior. Engineering turns that around: you have some behavior you would like to achieve, and you ask, what system could I build that would produce it? In that sense, engineering is an inverse problem.

And it’s generally not an inverse problem with a unique answer. There may be many systems that achieve your objective, with different costs, different robustness properties, different consequences. So you have to think about constraints and tradeoffs, and even about whether you’ve specified the objective correctly.

That doesn’t mean engineering is simply applying science after the science is finished. Trying to build something can expose fundamental questions that you wouldn’t have encountered just by observing what already exists. The two activities feed into each other.

r001.rationale: It describes engineering as starting with a desired behavior and working backward to a system that could produce it, calling this an inverse problem.

r002.rationale: It describes science as studying an existing system and explaining its behavior, but does not clearly state the forward direction from a given setup to a predicted outcome.

sol-6.1.text:
Well, in science, you’re often given a system that exists in the world, and you’re trying to understand it. You observe what it does, you propose mechanisms, and you try to work out which mechanisms could have produced those observations. That’s an inverse problem: from effects back to causes.

In engineering, you’re asking a related but different question: what system should I build to produce some desired behavior? You have an outcome in mind, and you work backward toward a design. There may be many designs that achieve that outcome, so you need to consider cost, robustness, constraints, and tradeoffs.

So I wouldn’t make the distinction simply that science solves inverse problems and engineering doesn’t. Both do. The distinction is more about the objective: are you trying to explain a system that exists, or create a system that does something useful? And, of course, those activities feed into each other.

r001.rationale: It says engineering starts with a desired behavior and works backward toward a design that will produce it.

r002.rationale: It describes science as reasoning backward from observed effects to possible causes, not forward from a setup to a predicted outcome.
